newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Palm Oil - Southeast Asian prices seen mixed.
newsitem.headline: Palm Oil - Southeast Asian prices seen mixed.

text.p: Malaysian palm oil prices are expected to soften this week on profit-taking and a lack of fresh fundamental factors, but Indonesia's market could see gains on continued buying, regional traders said.
Malaysian traders said they expected the market to consolidate as players await Malaysian crop forecaster Ivan Wong's estimates of palm oil production and stock in October, to be released this week.
"I think prices are on a downtrend as the rise (last) week appeared to be overdone," said a dealer in Kuala Lumpur.

Malaysian palm oil prices rose substantially through most of last week, driven mainly by speculative buying. But the market gave up some ground on Friday, when prices finished the year's heaviest trading session in negative territory.

Cargo surveyor Caleb Brett's estimate of October palm oil exports at 729,626 tonnes, released on Friday, was discounted by the market, traders said. Another cargo surveyor, Societe Generale de Surveillance (SGS) had put October exports at 736,374 tonnes, earlier last week.
The numbers from SGS helped the market extend its upswing ahead of Friday's session.
The traders said they expected January crude palm oil futures to trade in the 1,120 ringgit to 1,180 ringgit range this week.

The third position January crude palm oil futures contract ended down 11 ringgit at 1,170 ringgit ($463.00) a tonne on Friday after trading between 1,166 and 1,200. For the week, the contract was up 52 ringgit.
Vegetable oil dealers in Singapore reinforced the outlook from Malaysia. They said palm oil prices may undergo a correction this week after recent sharp gains on the bullish October export data.
"The market has been moving up quite sharply so it should slide down in a correction," a dealer in a Western commodity house said.

"Indian demand is beginning to dry up. You see China picking up other vegetable oils because they are increasingly finding palm more expensive. The trend looks soft," a trader in a commodity trading company said.
Other traders said a fall in soyoil prices in the United States may also pressure palm prices.
The Singapore market will also look closely at Ivan Wong's estimates of palm oil production and stocks for October for further direction, the traders said.
However, traders in Jakarta said Indonesian palm olein prices are expected to trend higher this week on continued buying interest.
They added indications of a tightening in supply of prompt-delivery olein could also help the market maintain last week's rebound after several weeks of declines.
"I see some upside potential in prices (this) week," one Indonesian trader said. "I think prices can go up to 1,400 rupiah where it will likely face some resistance."
Traders said there had been some renewed buying interest in the wake of last week's gains in Malaysia.
"When prices were falling (locally), buyers were mostly staying at the sidelines. But once prices started rising in Malaysia, they started coming back into the market," another trader said.
Palm olein prices finished on Friday at 1,375-80 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, up from 1,345-50 rupiah the previous week.
(with contributions from K.T. Arasu in Jakarta and Rene Pastor in Singapore)
